Before you start

Students learn why small exclusions hurt and why the first read is often off, then sort a situation into accident, drift, or on purpose. Bring scrap paper and index cards, count off for pairs so nobody is odd one out, and take deliberate, repeated exclusion to a counselor.

Every student in the room

Family rules, faith, money, rides and two-home weekends all mean some students miss more plans, and Nadia's partner can be any gender.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Open plainly: “Nobody names real people or real plans today. This is about the edge of the group.”

Slide 2 · Notes

First, everyone guesses a number in their head. Then eyes closed, hands up; you count out loud. The next slide shows what usually happens.

Slide 3 · Notes

Ask: “Why does it feel like everyone sees it?” Most people are busy thinking about themselves, and some of them feel on the edge too.

Slide 4 · Notes

Ask: “If a game with strangers stings, what about your actual friends?” The hurt is real and quick.

Slide 5 · Notes

Ask: “Which one hits hardest for you?” Answer in your head. Then: hurt first, and then your brain hunts for a reason.

Slide 6 · Notes

Name the trap: pulling back feels safe, and it also makes it easier for people to forget you, which confirms the feeling.

Slide 7 · Notes

Pairs by seat decide; anyone can pass. The next slide shows the read. Partner can be any gender.

Slide 8 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 9 · Notes

The next slide shows the likely read. Ask: “What’s the cost of assuming it was on purpose?”

Slide 10 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 11 · Notes

The next slide shows the read. Then name what backfires: disappearing to see who notices, keeping score, making people choose.

Slide 12 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 13 · Notes

People read disappearing as busy, not hurt. Muting a story notifies nobody, and turning off the map often feels easier than watching it.

Slide 14 · Notes

Private. Keep it about how it felt, with no list of what they did. In person or on a call works better than the group chat.

Slide 15 · Notes

Private, nobody shares: “What makes plans harder for you, or for people you know?” Treat it as logistics, not a flaw.

Slide 16 · Notes

Turn and talk, partners by seat. Then ask: “Where else in your life does this show up?” Nobody speaks for a group.

Slide 17 · Notes

Pick one in your head. Share the take-home link after: the check, the moves, and who to talk to.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why small exclusions hurt and why the first read on them is often off, sort a situation into accident, drift, or on purpose, and draft one honest sentence they could say to a friend. Nobody names real people or plans.

Materials

  • Scrap paper and a hat or bag for the anonymous guess
  • Index cards for the private honest sentence
  • The student page link (last slide) to share after advisory

Flow

  1. 5 minThe guess (anonymous cards)
  2. 5 minWhat exclusion does, and check first
  3. 5 minAccident, drift, or on purpose? (pairs)
  4. 3 minOne honest sentence (private)
  5. 2 minOne move and the student page

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

The guess (3), accident, drift, or on purpose with one scenario (3), one honest sentence (2), one move and the student page (2).

Before you teach
It may be happening in this circle.

Advisory groups are small, and the student on the edge of a friend group may be sitting near that group. Don't ask for real examples, names, or plans. Use only the slide scenarios.

Make pairing easy.

Being the odd one out is the topic, so don't let students choose partners. Count off, and join a pair yourself if the numbers are uneven.

On purpose, again and again, is bullying.

If a student describes being deliberately left out, rumors, or someone telling others not to hang out with them, thank them, move on, and follow up privately that day with a counselor or dean.

Weeks of feeling low go to a counselor.

The student page names feeling low or alone for weeks as a reason to get help. Don't ask about this in the circle. Any disclosure goes to a counselor the same day.

Jealousy is allowed.

Students may admit they're jealous of a friend's new friend or partner. Treat it as a sign the friendship matters and keep shame out of it.

Leave room for students who did the leaving out.

Some students have started a separate chat or forgotten someone. Give them a way in: a quick "want to come?" fixes a lot of accidents.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Family rules and faith shape plans.

Curfews, religious services and holy days, family responsibilities, and rules about where students can go mean some miss more plans. Present "I usually can't do Friday nights, but I'm in for Saturday afternoons" as a strong move, and don't assume every family runs the same way.

Money, jobs and rides.

Some students work, can't afford the plan, or don't have a ride. The "car with four seats" example fits here. When you model making a plan, suggest free ones.

Dating examples include everyone.

Nadia's partner Chris could be any gender; say "partner" or "someone you like" when you talk about it. A Close Friends list or a screenshot can also reveal who someone likes, which makes it a counselor conversation and never a discussion topic.

Social cues and social energy.

Autistic students, students with ADHD, and students with social anxiety may find it harder to tell whether a plan was open, or to walk up and sit down. The one honest sentence gives a script. Don't treat speaking up in the group as the only sign of a good friend.

Two homes, two schedules.

Students who split time between households, live with grandparents, or are in foster or kinship care may miss plans on certain weekends. Say "the adults at home" and treat it as logistics.

New to the group, the school, or the country.

Students who are new, or who speak another language at home, may feel on the edge when inside jokes and fast talk fly by. Widening your base can include a cultural club, a cousin, or an online group in their language.

What the research says

Psychologist Kipling Williams's model says being ignored or left out threatens four needs: belonging, self-esteem, control, and a sense that your presence matters ("meaningful existence").

Williams, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 2009

The model describes stages. The first two (the quick hurt, then a reflective stage) are well studied in experiments. The third, resignation, comes mostly from interviews and long-term observation, so it's less certain.

Williams, 2009

1,486 people from 62 countries played an online ball toss with two "players" who were really a computer. Those who stopped getting the ball felt worse and reported a weaker sense of belonging, even with strangers in a game that didn't matter.

Williams, Cheung and Choi, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2000

Cornell students who wore an embarrassing T-shirt into a room guessed about half the room would notice. About a quarter did.

Gilovich, Medvec and Savitsky, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2000

In a survey of 540 adults, people in a romantic relationship had smaller close support networks. Even counting the new partner, they had lost about two close people on average.

Burton-Chellew and Dunbar, Evolutionary Behavioral Sciences, 2015

Being left out hits control in particular, because it happens to you. That's why doing something about it, like making a plan yourself, often helps.

Williams, 2009
